mcqs.question: A user reports never receiving a push notification. Why can't this be diagnosed by checking only your backend's send logs?
options: Backend logs always fully determine delivery outcome

The push travels through three separate systems — your server, the platform push service, and the device OS — and a successful send from your server only confirms the first hop, not delivery through the other two
Push notifications don't use a backend server at all
The device always logs delivery failures back to your server automatically
mcqs.explanation: A confirmed send from your server only proves the first of three hops succeeded — the push service still has to reach the device, and the OS still has to decide to display it, either of which can silently fail with nothing surfaced back to your server automatically.

mcqs.question: An app relies solely on a silent/data push to trigger a critical, user-visible alert with no visible notification and no fallback check. What's the risk?
options: Silent pushes are more reliable than notification pushes, so this is actually the safer choice
There is no added risk; silent and notification pushes have identical delivery guarantees
Silent pushes deliver instantly with zero delay compared to notification pushes

Silent pushes are often deprioritized or coalesced more aggressively by the OS than user-visible ones, so relying on one alone for something the user must see reliably risks silent, undetected message loss
mcqs.explanation: Because a silent push has no visible UI holding the OS accountable, platforms reserve more latitude to drop or coalesce it under resource pressure — using it as the sole trigger for something critical means a dropped push produces no visible failure for anyone to catch.

mcqs.question: Why do push services deliberately coalesce or drop pending messages under load instead of queuing every message indefinitely?
options: Because they are optimized for timeliness at scale rather than guaranteed delivery, and indefinite queuing would conflict with that design goal
Because devices can only receive one push notification per day
Because backend servers are not allowed to send more than one push per user
Because coalescing is a bug that vendors have not yet fixed
mcqs.explanation: Push services are explicitly designed around timely best-effort delivery at massive scale, which means dropping or collapsing pending messages under pressure rather than guaranteeing every one is eventually delivered — this is deliberate, not a defect, and it's why any feature needing guaranteed correctness needs a fallback pull.

mcqs.question: Why does asking for notification permission immediately on first app launch typically produce worse opt-in rates than a soft-ask approach?
options: The OS blocks permission prompts during the first session
First-launch prompts are technically slower to render than later ones
The user has no context yet for why notifications would help them, so they're more likely to deny — and a denial is effectively unrecoverable without a settings deep-link
Soft-asks are required by app store policy before the real prompt
mcqs.explanation: A user asked before they understand the value has no reason to say yes, and because a denial usually sticks without the user manually changing settings later, that one shot at the real OS prompt is effectively burned. A soft-ask first, explaining the value with your own UI, improves the odds of a yes on the real prompt.

mcqs.question: A chat app relies purely on silent push to sync new messages, with no other sync mechanism. What's the architectural error?
options: Push should be a hint that something changed, not the sole transport for the data itself — any dropped or coalesced push becomes permanent, invisible data loss without a fallback sync path
Chat apps should never use push notifications at all
Silent pushes should be replaced entirely with notification pushes
The error is only that the UI doesn't show a loading spinner while waiting
mcqs.explanation: Treating push as the transport itself rather than a wake-up hint means every dropped push is permanent, undetected message loss from the user's perspective — the standard fix is combining push for timeliness with a real sync-on-foreground or periodic sync path that queries the actual source of truth.

mcqs.question: A checkout screen crashes when entered via deep link but works fine through normal in-app navigation. What's the most likely cause?
options: Deep links are inherently incompatible with checkout flows
The screen assumes state populated by a predecessor screen in normal navigation (like a selected address), which a deep link skips entirely by jumping straight to the destination
The deep link URI is malformed and needs better validation
The crash is unrelated to deep linking and is a rendering bug
mcqs.explanation: Deep links jump straight to a destination screen with none of the state a normal navigation path would have already built up, so a screen that implicitly assumes a predecessor already ran breaks — the fix is making every deep-linkable screen self-sufficient, fetching what it needs directly rather than assuming it's already there.
